front: What was the impact of Presidential Reconstruction on African American rights?
p1: Johnson issued mass pardons to Southern whites → Confederate land returned → '40 acres and a mule' never realised.
p2: Black Codes introduced by Southern states → restricted movement, labour, property rights → de facto re-enslavement.
p3: Johnson actively opposed 14th and 15th Amendments → vetoed both → Congress overruled him.

front: What were the key achievements of Radical Reconstruction?
p1: 14th Amendment (1868) → citizenship + equal protection. 15th Amendment (1870) → voting rights for Black men.
p2: Reconstruction Act (1867) → South divided into military districts → Black Codes removed → elections enforced.
p3: 1,500+ African Americans held public office → 22 in Congress → Blanche Bruce: full Senate term for Mississippi.

front: Why did Reconstruction fail?
p1: Hayes–Tilden Compromise (1877) → federal troops withdrawn → 'Redeemer' governments retook the South.
p2: Deaths of Sumner and Stevens + Panic of 1873 → Northern attention shifts → Radical Republican majority diluted.
p3: Slaughterhouse Case (1873) → civil rights ruled a state issue → Supreme Court undermined 14th Amendment.

front: What was the impact of Jim Crow laws on African American political rights?
p1: Spread across South from 1877 → segregated schools, transport, hospitals, parks, restaurants, churches.
p2: Voter suppression from 1890 → literacy tests, poll taxes, grandfather clauses → Mississippi Black voter registration: 90% (1867) → 6% (1892).
p3: Plessy v Ferguson (1896) → 'separate but equal' constitutional → gave legal cover to all Jim Crow legislation.

front: What was the significance of the Wilmington Coup (1898)?
p1: White supremacists violently overthrew the biracial elected government of Wilmington, North Carolina.
p2: Showed that even legitimate political power could be destroyed by organised white violence without federal protection.
p3: Mississippi v Williams (1898) same year → Supreme Court ruled voter suppression didn't violate 15th Amendment → over 90% disenfranchised by 1900.

front: What was the significance of Booker T. Washington?
p1: Atlanta Compromise (1895) → accepted social segregation in exchange for economic co-operation → critics saw this as legitimising Jim Crow.
p2: 'Tuskegee Machine' → controlled Black newspapers, charities, political appointments → first Black informal presidential advisor (Roosevelt, 1901).
p3: Du Bois argued Washington sacrificed political rights → founded Niagara Movement (1905) in direct opposition → later NAACP (1909).

front: What was the significance of W.E.B. Du Bois?
p1: Rejected Washington's accommodationism → demanded immediate full civil and political equality → 'talented tenth' must lead.
p2: Founded Niagara Movement (1905) → direct predecessor to NAACP. Co-founded NAACP (1909) → focused on legal litigation and political pressure.
p3: Edited The Crisis → promoted Black intellectualism and cultural achievement → 100,000 circulation by 1920s.

front: What was the strategy and significance of the NAACP?
p1: Founded 1909 → Du Bois, Ida B. Wells + white progressives → legal litigation + political pressure strategy.
p2: Key victories: US v Guinn (1915) → grandfather clauses unconstitutional. Smith v Allwright (1944) → all-white primaries banned → Black voter registration 2% (1940) → 12% (1947).
p3: Brown v Board (1954) → Thurgood Marshall proved $43/yr Black vs $179/yr white → 'separate but equal' overturned. Little Rock Nine (1957) organised.

front: What was the significance of Marcus Garvey and UNIA?
p1: Founded UNIA New York branch (1917) → The Negro World newspaper → 200,000 weekly readers. Black Star Line (1919) → 'Back to Africa' movement.
p2: UNIA reached 4 million members by early 1920s → largest Black mass movement in history → Black nationalism + Pan-Africanism.
p3: 'Garvey must go' campaign (1922) after meeting KKK → deported to Jamaica (1927) for mail fraud → federal government action ended movement.

front: What was the role of State Governments in hindering African American political rights?
p1: 'State Rights' ideology → argued states should manage affairs without federal interference → used to block civil rights enforcement.
p2: Massive resistance to Brown (1954) → Virginia closed all public schools rather than integrate → 300+ private 'segregation academies' founded.
p3: Wallace: 'segregation today, tomorrow, forever' → stood in University of Alabama doorway 1963. Faubus deployed National Guard against Little Rock Nine (1957).

front: What was the impact of the New Deal on African American political rights?
p1: FDR created informal 'Black Cabinet' → led by Mary McLeod Bethune → influenced New Deal programmes for Black Americans.
p2: Eleanor Roosevelt advocated for civil rights + supported anti-lynching bills. African Americans began voting Democratic in large numbers → major long-term political shift.
p3: Anti-Communist Red Scare → organisations improving AA rights suspected of communism → Du Bois surveilled + harassed → CIO lost funding.

front: What was the significance of the Warren Court (1953–1969)?
p1: Chief Justice Earl Warren → considered most liberal Supreme Court in US history → transformed federal protection of civil rights.
p2: Brown v Board (1954) → overturned Plessy. Browder v Gayle (1956) → segregated buses unconstitutional. Boynton v Virginia (1960) → interstate buses desegregated.
p3: Swann v Charlotte-Mecklenburg (1971) → bussing constitutional. Griggs v Duke Power Co. (1971) → affirmative action constitutional.

front: What was the impact of Brown v Board of Education (1954)?
p1: Thurgood Marshall proved Southern states spent $43/yr on Black students vs $179/yr white → Supreme Court overturned 'separate but equal'.
p2: Theoretically impacted 9 million Black children in the South → but no de facto change immediately → by 1964, 98% still attended segregated schools.
p3: Triggered 'massive resistance' across the South → Virginia closed schools → 300+ segregation academies founded → exposed limits of legal victories.

front: What was the strategy and significance of the SCLC?
p1: Founded 1957 → led by Martin Luther King → non-violent direct action → used media + moral pressure to force federal response.
p2: Birmingham Campaign (1963) → Bull Connor's violence vs peaceful protesters → broadcast nationwide → Kennedy announces moral duty to act → Civil Rights Act 1964.
p3: Selma March (1965) → 50% Black population, 1% electorate → Bloody Sunday broadcast nationally → directly led to Voting Rights Act 1965.

front: What was the strategy and significance of SNCC?
p1: Founded 1960 → grassroots, student-led → more radical than SCLC → organised sit-ins, Freedom Rides, voter registration drives.
p2: Selma March (1965) → John Lewis led marchers onto Edmund Pettus Bridge → 'Bloody Sunday' → Voting Rights Act.
p3: 1966 under Stokely Carmichael → rejected non-violence + integration → embraced Black Power → 'Black Power' slogan coined.

front: What was the Albany Campaign (1962) and why did it fail?
p1: SCLC and King targeted Albany, Georgia → Police Chief Laurie Pritchett used non-violent policing → denied King media images of brutality.
p2: No single dramatic confrontation → media lost interest → federal government had no reason to intervene → no legislation resulted.
p3: Key lesson → non-violent direct action only worked when it provoked visible repression on camera → shaped Birmingham Campaign strategy.

front: What were the Greensboro Sit-ins (1960) and why were they significant?
p1: 4 Black students sat at 'white-only' lunch counter in Greensboro, NC → spontaneous non-violent direct action.
p2: Over 70,000 students engaged in sit-ins across the South co-ordinated by SNCC → more than 1,000 businesses desegregated lunch counters.
p3: Demonstrated power of youth-led spontaneous protest → led to founding of SNCC → showed NAACP's legal approach could be complemented by direct action.

front: What were the Freedom Rides (1961) and what did they achieve?
p1: CORE + SNCC → Black and white activists rode interstate buses from Washington D.C. into the Deep South → testing Boynton v Virginia (1960).
p2: Met with violent mobs including fire-bombings in Alabama → national outrage → federal government forced to respond.
p3: Attorney General enforced desegregation of interstate public transport → demonstrated that federal pressure could be forced through confrontation.

front: What was the significance of the Birmingham Campaign (1963)?
p1: King + SCLC targeted Birmingham → Bull Connor used police dogs + fire hoses against peaceful protesters including children → images broadcast worldwide.
p2: Kennedy announced America had a 'moral duty' to intervene → directly led to Civil Rights Act 1964.
p3: Baptist Church bombings (1963) → KKK killed four young girls → no convictions → highlighted state government complicity in racial terror.

front: What was the significance of the March on Washington (1963)?
p1: 250,000 marched for jobs and freedom → King's 'I Have a Dream' speech → largest civil rights demonstration in US history.
p2: Organised by Randolph + Rustin → brought together NAACP, SCLC, SNCC, CORE, NUL → demonstrated broad coalition.
p3: Malcolm X dismissed it as a 'farce' → highlighted divisions between integrationist and nationalist wings of the movement.

front: What was the impact of the Civil Rights Act (1964)?
p1: Removed all Jim Crow segregation across the South → prohibited employment discrimination based on race.
p2: Pushed through by LBJ using 'Johnson treatment' → most significant federal civil rights legislation since Reconstruction.
p3: Limitations → did not address de facto segregation in the North → did not solve economic inequality → enforcement remained weak in many states.

front: What happened during the Selma March and what did it achieve?
p1: Selma: 50% Black population but only 1% of electorate → SCLC + SNCC march to expose voter suppression.
p2: Bloody Sunday → John Lewis led marchers → violent police attack on Edmund Pettus Bridge → broadcast nationwide.
p3: Directly led to Voting Rights Act (1965) → banned all voter suppression → Mississippi Black voter registration: 6% (1964) → 60% (1969).

front: What were the key ideas of Malcolm X and the Nation of Islam?
p1: NOI → Black nationalism + separatism → rejected integration → 'by any means necessary' → self-defence against white supremacy.
p2: NOI grew from 400 members (1952) → 40,000 (1960) under Malcolm X → addressed Northern urban poverty King's movement neglected.
p3: Post-Hajj (1964) → Malcolm X adopted more inclusive vision → broke from NOI → assassinated by NOI members 1965 → became martyr for Black Power.

front: What were the key ideas of Stokely Carmichael and Black Power?
p1: 1966 → took over SNCC → rejected non-violence + integration → coined 'Black Power' slogan during Meredith March.
p2: Black Power = self-determination, Black pride, economic self-sufficiency, community control — not dependence on white liberals.
p3: Alienated white allies + moderate African Americans → CORE lost white funding 1969 → weakened cross-racial coalition that had passed 1964/65 legislation.

front: Why did Black Power rise to prominence in the late 1960s?
p1: Failures of CRM in North → SCLC/NAACP focused on Southern desegregation → Northern urban communities still faced poverty + police violence. King's Chicago (1966) failed.
p2: Vietnam War → African Americans disproportionately drafted → returned radicalised → war severed King–LBJ relationship → media attention shifted.
p3: Long Hot Summers → Watts (1965) $40m damage → 150 riots (1967) → showed non-violence couldn't address systemic Northern inequality.

front: What was the impact of Nixon's 'War on Drugs' and Reagan's policies on African American political rights?
p1: Nixon's 'Law and Order' platform (1968) → War on Drugs → disproportionately targeted African Americans → mass incarceration begins.
p2: Reagan (1981–89) → Supreme Court became increasingly conservative → affirmative action labelled 'reverse discrimination' → federal enforcement reduced.
p3: By 1992 → 25% of Black men in prison, on parole or probation → War on Drugs described by Nixon aide as targeting Black communities deliberately.

front: What was the political position of African Americans by 1992?
p1: 8,000+ African Americans held public office → Congressional Black Caucus: 36 members → Thurgood Marshall (1967–91) first Black Supreme Court Justice. Douglas Wilder first Black governor (Virginia, 1989).
p2: Voter turnout 54% vs 61% white → unofficial suppression continued → gerrymandering + insufficient polling locations in Black areas.
p3: Jesse Jackson's 1984 + 1988 presidential campaigns won 7 million votes → but never official Democrat candidate → no Black presidential or VP candidate in the period.

front: What was the impact of the Freedmen's Bureau on African American social rights?
p1: Established 1865 → helped create 1,000+ Black schools → 250,000 enrolled → founded Howard University (1867), one of first HBCUs.
p2: Distributed 21 million rations of food to freedmen → provided basic housing, medical care and legal support.
p3: Closure 1872 → gains immediately reversed → educational and social progress lost without federal infrastructure to sustain it.

front: What was the impact of KKK terror during and after Reconstruction?
p1: KKK founded Tennessee 1865 → used violence to intimidate African Americans from voting, education, asserting rights.
p2: Colfax Massacre (1873) → c.100 African Americans killed in Louisiana following contested elections → federal government failed to help. New Orleans Massacre (1866): 40–200 killed.
p3: Enforcement Acts (1870–71) → Grant suppressed 1st KKK → over 600 prosecuted. But after 1877 troop withdrawal → KKK resurgent + unpunished.

front: What was the impact of lynching on African American social rights?
p1: Lynching epidemic → 100+ per year in early 1890s → used as tool of racial terror to enforce social hierarchy and deter political participation.
p2: Ida B. Wells → 'Southern Horrors' (1892) → documented frequency + disproved myth it was response to violent crime → national + international campaign.
p3: Southern Democratic politicians repeatedly defeated anti-lynching bills in Congress. In 1900, Governor Tillman of South Carolina openly defended lynching.

front: What was the impact of convict leasing on African Americans?
p1: Exploited 13th Amendment loophole → 'except as punishment for crime' → Southern states arrested African Americans on trivial charges → leased to private companies as unpaid labour.
p2: Grew across the South in the 1880s → effectively recreated slavery → dangerous conditions, no pay, no rights.
p3: System designed to control Black population + provide cheap labour to Southern economies → continued into early 20th century.

front: What was the role of anti-civil rights groups in hindering African American rights?
p1: KKK → violence at poll booths, lynching, destruction of Black organisations → Colfax Massacre (1873): 100+ killed to prevent voting.
p2: White Citizens Councils (1955) → 'respectable' opposition to integration → pressured employers, banks and landlords to discriminate → counterpart to KKK in the 1950s–60s.
p3: United Daughters of the Confederacy → 'Lost Cause' myth → romanticised slavery + Confederacy → justified Jim Crow → shaped Southern white opinion for generations.

front: What was the role of Social Darwinism and the 'Lost Cause' myth?
p1: 'Lost Cause' myth → Southern historians + United Daughters of the Confederacy → romanticised slavery + Confederacy → justified Jim Crow as natural social order.
p2: Social Darwinism → pseudoscientific extension of Darwin → eugenics seen as modern science → justified racial separation + hostility to interracial marriage.
p3: Media spread ideas of lazy, idle freedmen + myth of Black male sexual violence → reinforced white supremacy + justified lynching in public discourse.

front: What was the significance of Birth of a Nation (1915)?
p1: D.W. Griffith's film → glorified KKK → depicted Black men as threats to white women → early blockbuster seen by millions.
p2: Directly caused resurgence of KKK → membership reached c.5 million by 1920s → 15% of eligible population.
p3: Demonstrated power of media to entrench white supremacy → 19th century newspapers had already perpetuated stereotypes of Black criminality and sexual violence.

front: What was the impact of WWI service on African American social rights?
p1: 380,000 African Americans served in segregated units → Harlem Hellfighters → hoped military service would demonstrate citizenship + earn equal treatment.
p2: Many African American GIs stationed in Britain → experienced less segregated society → raised expectations on return.
p3: Red Summer (1919) → return of white soldiers + industrial retraction → race riots across America → worst violence in Chicago → African Americans fought back.

front: What was the significance of the Harlem Renaissance?
p1: 1920s cultural explosion → Langston Hughes, Louis Armstrong, Zora Neale Hurston → Black artistic achievement gained national recognition.
p2: Harlem population grew 50,000 → 200,000 (1910–1930) → Du Bois used The Crisis to promote Black intellectualism → 100,000 circulation.
p3: Cultural flourishing did not translate into political or economic gains → KKK at 5 million same decade → Tulsa massacre (1921) destroyed 'Black Wall Street'.

front: What was the impact of the Tulsa Race Massacre (1921)?
p1: White mob destroyed Greenwood District ('Black Wall Street') → 600+ Black-owned businesses destroyed → 35 blocks burned.
p2: Up to 300 African Americans killed → 10,000 left homeless → one of worst incidents of racial violence in US history.
p3: Showed that Black economic success provoked violent white backlash → prosperity offered no protection without political and legal rights.

front: What was the impact of the Great Depression on African American social rights?
p1: Black unemployment 50% vs 25% national average → 75% of Southern African Americans still sharecroppers → Depression hit hardest.
p2: 50+ African Americans lynched annually in 1920s → KKK at 5 million → social conditions remained deeply hostile throughout.
p3: Nation of Islam founded (1930) → offered alternative social vision of Black self-sufficiency → response to Depression despair + continued white supremacy.

front: What was the significance of the Double V Campaign?
p1: NAACP launched Double V → victory against fascism abroad AND racism at home → exposed contradiction of fighting for democracy while denying it domestically.
p2: NAACP membership grew 50,000 → 500,000 during WWII → Cold War context made federal government increasingly conscious of international optics.
p3: Soviet propaganda publicised racial violence like Birmingham Campaign → Kennedy: 'We preach freedom around the world… but are we to say the land of the free — except for the negroes?'

front: What was the impact of the Emmett Till case (1955)?
p1: 14-year-old boy from Chicago murdered in Mississippi → body mutilated → murderers acquitted by all-white jury.
p2: Mother insisted on open-casket funeral → allowed media to share images of Emmett's body → spread outrage nationally and internationally.
p3: Galvanised civil rights movement → demonstrated that racial terror was ongoing + systemic → key catalyst for Montgomery Bus Boycott.

front: What was the role of Cold War context in advancing African American civil rights?
p1: Soviet propaganda publicised US racial violence to discredit America internationally → Birmingham Campaign broadcast globally.
p2: Federal Government increasingly conscious of Cold War optics → Kennedy: 'land of the free — except for the negroes?' after Birmingham.
p3: Decolonisation movements in 1950s–60s inspired African Americans → Gandhi + Kwame Nkrumah's actions influenced non-violent strategy.

front: What was the role of the media in advancing the Civil Rights Movement?
p1: Televised images of Bloody Sunday (1965) + Birmingham Campaign (1963) shocked international audiences → generated massive support for movement.
p2: King adept at exploiting television cameras → chose Birmingham deliberately because Bull Connor guaranteed visible brutality → forced federal response.
p3: Emmett Till's open casket (1955) → media images of body spread outrage. Contrast with 19th century press → had perpetuated stereotypes + justified lynching.

front: What was the impact of Vietnam War on the Civil Rights Movement?
p1: African Americans disproportionately drafted → returned radicalised + disillusioned → fed Black Power ethos of militancy.
p2: King's 'Beyond Vietnam' speech (1967) → severed relationship with LBJ → ended federal momentum on civil rights reforms.
p3: Media attention shifted from civil rights marches to anti-war protests → movement lost national spotlight → Black Power filled the vacuum.

front: What was the impact of the Black Panther Party's community programmes?
p1: Free breakfast programmes → fed 20,000 children per day → 'survival programmes' addressed poverty the civil rights legislation had not solved.
p2: 13 health clinics established → screened thousands for sickle cell anaemia → People's Free Medical Centres in 13 deprived areas. 60+ community schools.
p3: BPP's 10-Point Programme demanded reparations, land, full employment, decent housing → shifted civil rights agenda from legal equality to economic justice.

front: What were the Long Hot Summers (1967) and what caused them?
p1: 150 race riots in 1967 → largest in Detroit and Newark → response to poverty, police brutality and de facto segregation in Northern cities.
p2: Watts (1965) $40m property damage → exposed failure of non-violence + civil rights legislation to address systemic Northern inequality.
p3: Showed CRM had not resolved economic grievances → MLK's assassination (1968) triggered new wave of riots → Nixon won on 'Law and Order' ticket.

front: What was the impact of COINTELPRO on Black Power organisations?
p1: FBI infiltrated Black Power groups → planted informants → manufactured evidence → created internal suspicion + divisions.
p2: Arrests + assassinations: Fred Hampton (Black Panther leader) killed in FBI-orchestrated raid 1969 → Panthers collapsed by 1982.
p3: Panthers never exceeded 5,000 members → COINTELPRO accelerated collapse → demonstrated state willingness to use illegal tactics against civil rights organisations.

front: What was the impact of Reagan's social policies on African Americans?
p1: Welfare cuts disproportionately harmed African Americans → deepened economic disparities → 33% below poverty line by 1992 vs 12% white.
p2: School desegregation reversed → judicial weakening of bussing → by 1992, 40% of Black students attended majority-Black schools → re-segregation.
p3: War on Drugs accelerated → mass incarceration → by 1992, 25% of Black men in prison, on parole or probation. HBCUs remained vital → produced 25% of Black graduates.

front: What was the significance of the Los Angeles Riots (1992)?
p1: Erupted after acquittal of LAPD officers for beating Rodney King by all-white jury → $1 billion of damage → 63 killed.
p2: Demonstrated that police brutality + racial injustice remained systemic → civil rights legislation had not changed ground realities for urban Black communities.
p3: Positive strides by 1992 → Oprah, Michael Jordan, Spike Lee as icons of Black success → but persistent stereotypes + poverty for majority remained.

front: Why did sharecropping trap African Americans in poverty?
p1: No land redistribution → '40 acres and a mule' never realised → freedpeople forced to farm same land, same landowner as during slavery.
p2: Crop-lien system → sharecroppers paid rent in crops → always in debt to landowner → could not leave without repaying debt → effective debt bondage.
p3: By 1900 only 25% of African Americans owned land → economic freedom impossible without land ownership → Southern economic system rebuilt on near-slavery.

front: What was the significance of Madam C.J. Walker?
p1: Built beauty empire for Afro hair in 1910s → employed thousands of Black women → became first self-made female millionaire in the USA.
p2: Demonstrated Black economic success possible despite Jim Crow → parallel economy serving Black customers → model for Black business development.
p3: Part of broader pattern → by 1890s 50,000+ Black-owned businesses → 40 Black-owned banks → 'Black towns' like Mound Bayou, Mississippi had 150+ businesses.

front: What was the significance of the Great Migration?
p1: 1916–1970 → over 6 million African Americans moved from rural South to Northern + Western cities → escaping Jim Crow + seeking economic opportunity.
p2: Created influential Black urban communities → Harlem + South Side Chicago → fostered cultural and political movements → WWI phase: 500,000 moved 1916–19.
p3: Opened skilled industrial jobs in North → 40% of Black men in North held skilled jobs by 1920 vs 15% in South → but de facto segregation + racial hostility persisted.

front: What was the significance of Philip Randolph and the BSCP?
p1: BSCP (Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters) founded 1925 → first successful Black union → led by Randolph → protected Pullman Company porters.
p2: First Black union to receive AFL recognition (1935) → secured contract 1937: higher wages, shorter hours, paid uniforms → proved Black workers could organise.
p3: March on Washington Movement (1941) → threatened 100,000-strong march → pressured FDR into Executive Order 8802 → banned discrimination in defence industries.

front: What was the impact of WWI on African American economic rights?
p1: Wartime demand for labour → Great Migration accelerated → 500,000 moved North 1916–19 → industrial wages significantly higher than sharecropping.
p2: Gains were short-lived → Red Summer (1919) → Elaine Massacre: Black sharecroppers organising for better wages → white mobs killed 200+ → gains reversed.
p3: Elaine Massacre showed → economic organising by Black workers met with violent suppression → structural barriers remained regardless of wartime opportunity.

front: What was the impact of the Great Depression on African American economic rights?
p1: Black unemployment 50% vs 25% national average → 75% of Southern African Americans still sharecroppers → hardest hit community.
p2: Urban areas: Chicago Black unemployment 20% (1930) vs 12% white — before Depression's full impact. Jobs lost in North disproportionately held by African Americans.
p3: AFL had no affiliated Black unions → African Americans restricted to unprotected jobs → economic vulnerability exposed lack of union protection.

front: How did the First New Deal affect African Americans economically?
p1: FERA → direct relief → 20–30% of recipients were African American. CCC → employed c.200,000 African Americans (10% of enrolment). PWA → 65,000+ in infrastructure jobs by 1940.
p2: Some Black sharecroppers became independent farmers through federal assistance → Black Cabinet influenced programme delivery.
p3: AAA (1933) inadvertently displaced 200,000 Black sharecroppers → NRA codes manipulated by employers → gains were partial and unevenly distributed.

front: How did the Second New Deal affect African Americans?
p1: WPA → infrastructure jobs → 15% of workers were African American. Social Security Act → pensions + unemployment insurance for the first time.
p2: Wagner Act (1935) → recognised BSCP → first Black union to win AFL recognition → but inadvertently created 'closed shops' → white-only unions could dominate.
p3: Bethune's role in NYA → funded training + jobs for 600,000 Black youths during Depression → most direct targeted benefit for African Americans.

front: What were the economic limitations of the New Deal for African Americans?
p1: Social Security excluded agricultural + domestic workers → 65% of Black workers → most significant exclusion from New Deal economic protection.
p2: Aid administered by Southern states → whites controlled distribution → African Americans discriminated against in application of relief policies.
p3: Anti-Communist Red Scare → organisations advocating for Black economic rights suspected of communism → CIO lost funding → unions weakened.

front: What was the impact of Executive Order 8802 (1941) on African American economic rights?
p1: Randolph's March on Washington Movement threatened 100,000-strong march → pressured FDR → EO 8802 banned racial discrimination in defence industries.
p2: By end of WWII → 2 million+ African Americans employed in defence industries → significant wartime economic opportunity.
p3: First time a mass non-violent movement forced a major federal economic concession → model for later civil rights pressure tactics.

front: What was the impact of post-WWII automation on African American economic rights?
p1: Automation in manufacturing post-WWII → disproportionately affected African Americans → concentrated in low-skill manual labour jobs that were eliminated.
p2: Black unemployment double white rates throughout this period → Great Migration had brought African Americans into industrial jobs now being automated away.
p3: Shift to service economy accelerated → African Americans not positioned to benefit → economic bifurcation → growing middle class alongside persistent ghetto poverty.

front: What was the impact of the Great Society programmes on African American economic rights?
p1: Medicare + Medicaid (1965) → Black Americans with health insurance: 25% → 75% by 1970. Food Stamp Act (1964) → 33% of recipients were African American despite being 12% of population.
p2: Civil Rights Act (1964) → prohibited employment discrimination → EEOC enforcement → African Americans in white-collar jobs: 5% (1960) → 15% (mid-1970s).
p3: Despite legislation → by 1970 Black families earned average 58% of white families → CRM failed to make economic gains in Northern cities.

front: What was the strategy and significance of the NUL (National Urban League)?
p1: Founded 1910 → worked to improve access to jobs, housing and healthcare in Northern cities → helped 250,000 secure housing by 1960s.
p2: Whitney Young, NUL leader → advised LBJ on anti-poverty initiatives → economic focus complemented NAACP's legal strategy.
p3: Limitations → NUL approach seen as too moderate → focused on working within system → did not challenge structural racism directly.

front: What was the economic impact of Black Power and the DRUM/LRBW movement?
p1: DRUM (Dodge Revolutionary Union Movement, 1968) → organised wildcat strikes at Chrysler's Dodge Main plant → challenged racial pay gap in auto industry.
p2: LRBW (League of Revolutionary Black Workers) pushed for Black leadership in UAW → by early 1970s Black workers: 30% of UAW membership → more Black leaders in UAW + GM.
p3: Limitations → LRBW collapsed from internal divisions by early 1970s → Black workers earned $2,000 less/year than white counterparts → structural gap remained.

front: What was the impact of affirmative action on African American economic rights?
p1: First introduced Philadelphia 1969 → spread nationally → African Americans in white-collar jobs: 5% (1960) → 15% (mid-1970s) → growing Black middle class.
p2: Regents of University of California v Bakke (1978) → racial quotas unconstitutional → weakened programme. Reagan/Bush labelled it 'reverse discrimination' → federal enforcement reduced.
p3: By 1980s → 40% of African Americans middle class → but gains uneven → 'bifurcation' → persistent ghetto poverty alongside professional success.

front: What was the economic position of African Americans by 1992?
p1: African Americans earned 60% of average white income → Black unemployment 14.2% vs 7.2% white → overrepresented in low-wage sectors.
p2: Homeownership 43% vs 70% white → redlining + discriminatory lending had lasting effects → urban renewal projects displaced many Black communities.
p3: 500,000+ Black-owned businesses → $10 billion gross revenue → 40% middle class → but 33% below poverty line → 'bifurcation' defined economic reality by 1992.
